items.title: 21.6 Emission and Absorption Spectra from Different Stars

source_refs.note: Topic 21.6 with the Tidbit (PDF 174-175); Fig 21.5 redrawn. The check question is added; answer needs review.

blocks.text: Stars emit a continuous spectrum of light because their extremely hot, dense surfaces behave like near-perfect blackbodies. As this light passes through the cooler outer atmosphere of the star, atoms in the gaseous layers absorb specific wavelengths corresponding to electron transitions between energy levels. This creates dark lines in the continuous spectrum where particular colours have been absorbed: an absorption spectrum. Although the absorbed energy is re-emitted at the same wavelengths, the re-emitted photons are scattered in all directions, so few reach observers on Earth, and we detect a characteristic absorption spectrum with distinct missing wavelengths. The pattern of lines shows which elements a star is made of.

In the emission and absorption spectra of distant stars and galaxies, the lines show an increase in wavelength from their known laboratory values (Fig 21.5). This is called redshift, and it occurs because the light is stretched as it travels through the expanding universe.

blocks.alt: Two rainbow strips from violet (short wavelength) to red (long wavelength), each crossed by four dark absorption lines. In the top strip (light from the Sun) the lines are at their usual positions; in the lower strip (light from a distant galaxy) the same pattern of lines is shifted to the right, towards red, shown by red arrows. Below: z = dlambda/lambda = df/f = v/c for v much less than c.
blocks.caption: Redshift of spectral lines (original diagram after Fig 21.5).
blocks.long_description: The pattern of lines identifies the elements, and the whole pattern is shifted to longer wavelengths. The size of the shift gives the speed at which the galaxy is moving away.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Every star has its own light signature. By studying its emission and absorption spectra, scientists can determine what elements a star is made of.
